name: ParsPack
description: ParsPack markets hosting, cloud servers, storage, and related infrastructure services for businesses serving Iran and other locations. Its public documentation describes both browser-based resource management and an API for automating cloud-server operations.

seo.title: ParsPack: Hosting and Cloud Infrastructure in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore ParsPack's advertised cloud servers, storage, hosting, and developer API, with clear distinctions between product descriptions and verified performance.

content.heading: A provider spanning hosting and infrastructure
content.content:
ParsPack's product catalogue brings together website hosting, virtual and dedicated servers, cloud storage, content delivery, and platform services. For an international reader, this breadth matters: the company presents several ways to put a digital service online, rather than a single standardized cloud product. A small website and an application requiring control over its server environment would encounter different offerings within the same catalogue. [s1]

The company's own account dates its first cloud-service product to Farvardin 1388 in the Iranian Solar Hijri calendar. That is a statement about a product launch, and should not automatically be treated as its legal incorporation date. Its accompanying claims to national precedence and market leadership remain company assertions; the inspected material does not establish an independently measured market ranking. [s2]

content.heading: What the cloud-server offering describes
content.content:
The cloud-server page describes virtualized computing resources whose processor allocation, memory, and storage can be adjusted. It advertises Linux and Windows options, administrator-level access, and a panel for managing server state and viewing resource information. These features describe an environment in which customers can administer a server, rather than simply upload content to a managed website. [s3]

ParsPack also advertises domestic and overseas locations, including Iran and Germany. Location is therefore a product choice, not something that should be inferred from the provider's Iranian identity. Its pricing explanation links charges to the selected location and resources, while the frequently asked questions describe daily deductions from account credit. The page's broader consumption-based language should be read alongside those specific billing terms. Neither regional availability nor the cost of a particular configuration was tested for this article. [s3]

content.heading: Storage as a separate service
content.content:
ParsPack's storage page presents choices between Iran and Europe and between solid-state and hard-disk storage. It also advertises an S3-compatible interface, a file-management panel, and encrypted HTTPS connections. S3 compatibility concerns the interface used to work with stored objects; it does not mean that Amazon operates the service. [s4]

The storage offering is distinct from the disk attached to an individual cloud server. That distinction helps explain the catalogue: an application can require computing capacity and a separate place to retain files. The provider describes archival and backup uses, but this article has not independently verified retention behavior, restoration success, or the physical separation of copies. [s4]

content.heading: From a control panel to automation
content.content:
The developer guide describes an application programming interface, or API, for creating virtual machines, managing network settings, and retrieving server information. It documents token authentication and gives example HTTP requests. This makes the documentation relevant to teams that want repeatable infrastructure operations rather than only manual changes through a browser. [s5]

The guide is evidence of a documented interface, not an operational test of every endpoint. Read together, the catalogue and documentation establish the scope of ParsPack's advertised offering. They do not establish actual application availability, customer satisfaction, or comparative performance against other Iranian providers. [s1][s5]

name: Asiatech
description: Asiatech appears in Iran's infrastructure market through server hosting, colocation, and cloud-related services. Cloud.ir identifies Asiatech data centers as the physical foundation of its cloud infrastructure, illustrating the relationship between facilities and the services built on them.

seo.title: Asiatech: Data Centers, Colocation and Cloud Services | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Asiatech's advertised infrastructure role, its connection to Cloud.ir, and the distinction between server colocation and cloud services.

content.heading: Connecting facilities with digital services
content.content:
Asiatech's infrastructure role is visible in two complementary kinds of public material. Its self-described official communications channel advertises dedicated servers, cloud servers, dedicated bandwidth, and colocation. Cloud.ir's company profile separately states that its infrastructure runs on Asiatech data centers. Together, these sources describe both physical hosting and services delivered above that physical layer. [s1][s2]

This relationship is useful for understanding Iran's cloud market. A data center supplies the environment in which equipment operates; a cloud service supplies a way to obtain and manage computing resources. The two can be closely connected without being interchangeable. Cloud.ir's website attributes its rights to the company named Asr Dadehaye Asiatech, but the inspected page alone does not establish every legal or ownership relationship within the wider Asiatech business. [s2]

content.heading: Colocation starts with the customer's equipment
content.content:
Colocation means placing customer-owned servers in a provider's hosting environment. Asiatech's channel explicitly presents the service for businesses that have already bought servers and need data-center space and network access. Its descriptions mention environmental temperature and humidity management, fire detection and suppression, monitoring, and support. [s1]

These are advertised service features, rather than published inspection results. The distinction matters because buying space for an existing machine leaves a different set of responsibilities from renting a virtual server. The channel also lists dedicated-server and cloud-server services separately, indicating that customers are being offered different infrastructure arrangements. The inspected posts do not provide a complete contractual allocation of hardware, operating-system, or application responsibilities. [s1]

content.heading: Reading the Cloud.ir connection
content.content:
Cloud.ir's catalogue lists cloud servers, cloud data centers, cloud switches, domain management, content delivery, and cloud storage. These names indicate a portfolio covering computing, networking, and data delivery. They should not be treated as proof that every product is available in every facility or under identical service terms. [s3]

The provider's profile says that its cloud activity began in Solar Hijri year 1399. That statement concerns Cloud.ir's service history; it should not be substituted for an Asiatech incorporation date. The same profile places Cloud.ir infrastructure on Asiatech facilities and makes broad claims about standards and reliability. Those claims require facility-specific documents before they can support a certification statement about a named site. [s2]

content.heading: What the evidence establishes
content.content:
The documented connection between a cloud platform and an underlying facility helps explain the company's relevance beyond website hosting. It shows how a service catalogue can depend on a separate physical infrastructure layer. NIST's cloud definition provides a useful general distinction: cloud computing concerns on-demand access to a shared pool of configurable resources, rather than merely the presence of servers in a building. [s2][s4]

The strongest supported conclusion is therefore about Asiatech's advertised role in an infrastructure ecosystem. The inspected sources do not establish its national market share, independently measured service quality, or the capacity of individual sites. A fuller company account needs dated corporate disclosures and facility evidence, especially to describe the business precisely at the requested research cutoff.

name: Data Center Services
description: Data center services provide the physical environment and supporting infrastructure in which servers operate. In Iran, provider descriptions include colocation, server rental, and cloud-related services, but these arrangements assign different roles to the customer and the operator.

seo.title: Data Center Services in Iran: Facilities, Colocation and Cloud | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An introduction to Iranian data center services, customer-owned server colocation, cloud infrastructure, and the meaning and limits of Tier certification.

content.heading: The physical foundation of online services
content.content:
A data center is part of the physical foundation beneath online services. Power, cooling, and equipment distribution paths affect whether computing equipment can continue operating during maintenance or failures. Uptime Institute's infrastructure classifications focus on these capabilities, while its operational sustainability framework addresses the management practices that also influence outcomes. A building's equipment specification is therefore only part of the reliability question. [s1]

In the Iranian market, the phrase 'data center services' can cover several commercial arrangements. Asiatech's public channel distinguishes customer-owned server colocation from dedicated and cloud servers. ParsPack's enterprise page separately lists data-center space and database services. These examples establish a range of advertised offerings, rather than a complete inventory of Iranian facilities or their capacity. [s3][s4]

content.heading: Space, servers, and cloud resources
content.content:
Colocation begins with equipment the customer already owns. The provider supplies an environment in which to place it, together with contracted supporting services. Asiatech describes this arrangement for businesses that have purchased servers but need hosting space and network access; its promotional posts also mention environmental controls and fire protection. Those descriptions explain the service model without proving that a particular facility meets a particular performance threshold. [s3]

Cloud computing describes a different layer. NIST defines it around on-demand network access to pooled, configurable resources that can be provisioned and released with limited management effort. Renting rack space alone does not establish those cloud characteristics. A facility may host a cloud platform, customer equipment, or both, but its physical infrastructure and the customer's service interface remain distinct concepts. [s5]

content.heading: What a Tier claim can establish
content.content:
Uptime Institute distinguishes basic infrastructure, redundant capacity, concurrent maintainability, and fault tolerance within its Tier system. Concurrent maintainability concerns planned removal of components or distribution paths without interrupting operations. Fault tolerance adds protection against an individual equipment failure or distribution-path interruption. These are infrastructure capabilities, not interchangeable descriptions of application performance. [s1][s2]

Certification is a separate evidentiary step: Uptime Institute describes it as verification that the relevant standard has been applied. Its certification process distinguishes design documents, constructed facilities, and operational sustainability. An article should consequently identify the facility and certification scope before assigning a certified status. A provider's general reference to standards cannot establish all of those details. Nor does a facility classification, by itself, supply an annual record of customer-visible uptime. [s2]

content.title: From facilities to application services
content.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Facility power and cooling"] -->|"Support equipment operation"| B["Physical servers and networks"]
  B -->|"Host customer-owned equipment"| C["Colocation arrangement"]
  B -->|"Supply underlying resources"| D["Cloud resource pool"]
  D -->|"Provides configurable resources"| E["Customer cloud workloads"]
```
content.summary: This conceptual diagram separates physical support from service delivery. It does not describe a particular Iranian facility or imply that every colocation operator also offers cloud computing.

content.heading: Reading Iranian service descriptions carefully
content.content:
The inspected Iranian examples reveal different levels of detail. Asiatech's channel explains the intended colocation customer and supporting features. ParsPack's enterprise page identifies data-center space as an offering, but provides little facility-specific technical evidence in that section. It also lists database clustering and replication, illustrating how operational services can appear beside physical hosting in the same enterprise catalogue. [s3][s4]

For readers exploring the sector, the useful distinction is between what is being sold and what has been demonstrated. A catalogue establishes an offering; a facility document establishes a specified design or certification scope; an operational record establishes measured experience. The available evidence supports this explanation of service models, but a comprehensive account of Iran's regional capacity and operating performance still requires further research. [s2][s3][s4]
